topic.name: Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = 7\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 36.$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 6\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +6\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 6\cos t, \qquad y = 6\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= 7, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 2. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\cos t) = -6\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\sin t) = 6\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 7\right) \cdot \big(6\cos t \big) - \left( 2\right) \cdot \big( -6\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 42 \cos t + 12\sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= (42\sin t - 12 \cos t) \, \Big|_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= (0 - 12 ) -(0 - 12)\\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y^3\,\mathbf{i} + x^3\,\mathbf{j}$ across the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

\[ x^2 + y^2 = 1^2. \]

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos t, \qquad y = \sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y^3 = \sin^3 t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= x^3 = \cos^3 t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\cos t) = -\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sin t) = \cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\sin t, \textrm d u = \cos t \,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(\sin^3 t \right) \cdot \big( \cos t \big) - \left( \cos^3 t\right) \cdot \big( -\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \sin^3 t \cos t + \sin t \cos^3 t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \sin t \cos t (\sin^2 +\cos^2 t) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \sin t \cos t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{0} u \: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = x\,\mathbf{i} - 5 \,\mathbf{j}$ across the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 25.$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

\[ x^2 + y^2 = 5^2. \]

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $5.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 5\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 5\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 5\cos t, \qquad y = 5\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= x = 5\cos t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= -5. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\cos t) = -5\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\sin t) = 5\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 5\cos t \right) \cdot \big( 5\cos t \big) - \left(- 5 \right) \cdot \big( -5\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 25\cos^2 t - 25\sin t\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 25\int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{\cos(2t)+1}{2} - \sin t\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 25\left(\dfrac{\sin(2t)}{4} + \dfrac 12 t + \cos t\right) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= 25(0 + \pi + 1) - (0 + 1) \\[5pt] &= 25\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =4\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}$ through the curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = \dfrac{t}{2}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{1}{2t}\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[\dfrac{1}{2},2\right],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x. \] To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

  • the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ must be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

In this case, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x =\dfrac{t}{2}, \qquad y = \dfrac{1}{2t}. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= 4 , \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 2 . \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\dfrac{t}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\dfrac{1}{2t}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2t^2}. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \int\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} (4) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2t^2}\right) - (2) \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} -\dfrac{2}{t^2} - 1\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac{2}{t} - t \right)\Bigg|_{1/2}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \left( 1 - 2 \right) - \left( 4 - \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{9}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =3xy\,\mathbf{i} + (2x+1)\,\mathbf{j}$ through the curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} +t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[0,1\right],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x. \] To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

  • the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ must be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

In this case, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t, \qquad y = t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= 3xy = 3t^2, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 2x+1 = 2t+1 . \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left( t\right) = 1, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(t\right) = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \int\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} ( 3t^2 ) (1) - (2t+1)(1)\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} 3t^2 - 2t -1\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= (t^3-t^2-t)\Bigg|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= (1-1-1) - (0-0-0) \\[5pt] &= -1 \end{align*}
